texts.facts: In this case, a Detailed Accident Report was filed by police in terms of provisions of Motor Vehicle Act qua accident of Vishnu S/o Sh. Johri Lal (hereinafter called 'the claimant') and same is treated as Claim Petition in view of the Provisions contained under Section 166 (4) of the Motor Vehicle Act. 2. Preliminary information regarding accident in question was received at PS vide DD No. 59A dated 07.07.2017 by PCR call, upon receipt of which HC Harender MACT No 251/2018 Vishnu Vs. Jitender Page No. 2 o Kumar alongwith Ct. Gangaram rushed to spot near DESU Office, Sanjay Colony, where it was informed that injured has already been taken to hospital while TSR bearing Registration No.HR55V 9747 was found in accidental condition at the spot and TSR driver was also found caught by the public persons at the spot. Sh. Suresh, brother of injured was also found at the spot, who stated that he has witnessed the accident. DD No. 4A dated 08.09.2017 regarding MLC of injured was received from AIIMS Trauma Center, where patient Vishnu was found admitted and was opined to be unfit for giving statement due to mouth injury. FIR was registered on the basis of DD entry and MLC. Investigation was carried out. No CCTV camera was found installed at the spot. Offending vehicle was seized and mechanical inspection was got conducted. On 19.07.2017, MLC of injured was collected wherein injuries were opined to be grievous. Notice under Section 133 of M.V. Act was served upon registered owner, who stated that his TSR was taken away/repossessed by the Finance Company as he could not repay regular EMI towards loan and that he was not aware about the whereabouts of the TSR. Thereafter, notice under Section 160 Cr.P.C. was served upon Finance Company, fromwhere, it was disclosed that the offending vehicle (TSR) was sold out to one Hawa Singh S/o Sh. Hukam Singh and accordingly, notice u/s 160 Cr.P.C. was given to Hawa Singh, who further disclosed that he had sold the offending vehicle to one Ram Chandra Kumar S/o Sh. Ganesh Dutt. Said Ram Chandra Kumar joined the investigation and disclosed that he had also sold the TSR to one Amit Kumar S/o Sh. Shankar Singh. Thus, notice under Section 133 M.V. Act was given to last owner Amit Kumar, who admitted that he bought the said TSR from Ram Chandra Kumar and disclosed that at the time of accident, his cousin (Foofa Ka Ladka) Jitender Kumar S/o Bharat Bhagat was driving MACT No 251/2018 Vishnu Vs. Jitender Page No. 3 of 29 the TSR. Upon completion of investigation, charge-sheet was filed under Sections 279/338 IPC and under Section 3/181 and 146/196 of MV Act, against driver Jitender Kumar. DAR was filed by Investigating Officer before this Tribunal on Vishnu (Dar) vs Jitender (260/17 O.I. Area) on 4 January, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/114979208/ 2 11.01.2018. Since besides driver Jitender Kumar no one else was impleaded as respondent, directions were given by Ld. Predecessor of this Tribunal to implead all the possessors/owners i.e. Munir Ali, Hawa Singh, Ram Chander and Amit Kumar as respondents vide order dated 11.01.2018. 3. A common written statement has been filed on behalf respondent Hawa Singh, Ram Chander, Amit Kumar and Jitender. Registered Owner Munir Ali has also appeared before this Tribunal on 19.2.2018 and 27.02.2018, however thereafter he stopped appearing, as such, proceedings against him were proceeded ex-parte vide order dated 03.10.2018. 4. In the written statement filed of on behalf respondent Hawa Singh, Ram Chander, Amit Kumar and Jitender, it was stated that Muneer Ali is registered owner of the offending vehicle, as such, presentation of Amit Kumar as owner in possession is bad in the eyes of law. It was further stated that Hawa Singh and Ram Chander have no concern as they are neither the drivers nor the registered owner and hence, they are not liable to pay any compensation. It is prayed that the petition be dismissed. In the meanwhile, claimant has expired and his legal heirs were impleaded as claimants vide order dated 17.10.2023 upon an application. 7. Matter was then listed for Petitioner Evidence. Petitioner appeared as PW-1 and tendered his evidentiary affidavit as Ex.PW1/A and relied upon copy of DAR (Ex.PW1/1), medical treatment documents (Ex.PW1/2) and final report (Ex.PW1/3). Cross-examination was deferred as none appeared on behalf of any of the respondents for cross-examination of PW1. In the meanwhile, petitioner expired. His wife Laxmi appeared as PW2 and tendered her evidentiary affidavit as Ex.PW2/A and relied upon her Aadhar Card as Ex.PW2/1 and death certificate of her husband Vishnu as Ex.PW2/2. Similarly, brother of petitioner Raju appeared as eye-witness and tendered his affidavit as Ex.PW3/A and relied upon his Aadhar Card as Ex.PW3/1. Both these witnesses were not put to cross-examination by any of the respondents despite opportunity. Petitioner evidence was closed. 8. Matter was listed for Respondents Evidence which was also closed vide order dated 04.01.2024. None appeared on behalf of respondents to advance arguments. 15. Police after investigation had filed charge-sheet against respondent no.1 under Section 279/338 IPC which is also suggestive of negligence of respondent no.1 in causing the accident.
texts.arguments: In National Insurance Co. Vs. Pushpa Rana 2009 ACJ 287 Delhi, it was laid down that completion of investigation and filing of charge-sheet under relevant section are sufficient proof of negligence of the driver of the offending vehicle. 16. It is also settled that if driver of offending vehicle does not enter the witnes box, an adverse inference can be drawn against him as observed by Hon'ble High Court of India in the case of Cholamandlam Insurance Company Ltd. Vs. Kamlesh 2009 (3) AD Delhi 310. 17. OPP" 12. Sec. 168 MV Act enjoins the Claim Tribunals to hold an enquiry into the claim to make an effort determining the amount of compensation which appears to it to be just and reasonable. Same is reproduced hereunder for ready reference : "(1) Award of the Claims Tribunal.--On receipt of an application for compensation made under section 166, the Claims Tribunal shall, after giving notice of the application to the insurer and after giving the parties (including the insurer) an opportunity of being heard, hold an inquiry into the claim or, as the case may be, each of the claims and, subject to the provisions of section 162 may make an award determining the amount of compensation which appears to it to be just and specifying the person or persons to whom compensation shall be paid and in making the award the Claims Tribunal shall specify the amount which shall be paid by the MACT No 251/2018 Vishnu Vs. Jitender Page No. 8 of 2 insurer or owner or driver of the vehicle involved in the accident or by all or any of them, as the case may be: Provided that where such application makes a claim for compensation under section 140 in respect of the death or permanent disablement of any person, such claim and any other claim (whether made in such application or otherwise) for compensation in respect of such death or permanent disablement shall be disposed of in accordance with the provisions of Chapter X. (2) The Claims Tribunal shall arrange to deliver copies of the award to the parties concerned expeditiously and in any case within a period of fifteen days from the date of the award. (3) When an award is made under this section, the person who is required to pay any amount in terms of such award shall, within thirty days of the date of announcing the award by the Claims Tribunal, deposit the entire amount awarded in such manner as the Claims Tribunal may direct." The Divisional Manager United India Insurance Company Ltd, SLP (Civil) No. 19277 of 2019). 14. The basic principle in assessing motor vehicle compensation claims, is to place the victim in as near a position as she or he was in before the accident, with other compensatory directions for loss of amenities and other payments. These general principles have been stated and reiterated in several decisions. [Support drawn from Govind Yadav Vs. New India Insurance Company Ltd. reported as (2011) 10 SCC 683.] MACT No 251/2018 Vishnu Vs. Jitender Page No. 9 of 2 15. This Tribunal has been tasked with determination of just compensation. The observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Divisional Controller, KSRTC Vs. Mahadeva Shetty & Anr., reported as (2003) 7 SCC 197, needs mention here (para 15): "Statutory provisions clearly indicate that the compensation must be "just" and it cannot be a bonanza; not a source of profit but the same should not be a pittance. The courts and tribunals have a duty to weigh the various factors and quantify the amount of compensation, which should be just. What would be "just" compensation is a vexed question. There can be no golden rule applicable to all cases for measuring the value of human life or a limb. Measure of damages cannot be arrived at by precise mathematical calculations. It would depend upon the particular facts and circumstances, and attending peculiar or special features, if any. Every method or mode adopted for assessing compensation has to be considered in the background of "just" compensation which is the pivotal consideration. Though by use of the expression "which appears to it to be just", a wide discretion is vested in the Tribunal, the determination has to be rational, to be done by a judicious approach and not the outcome of whims, wild guesses and arbitrariness.. ..." 16. Delineating the damages as pecuniary and non pecuniary, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, in case of R. D. Hattangadi Vs. Pest Control (India) Pvt Ltd, 1995 AIR 755, made following observations: "9....while fixing an amount of compensation payable to a victim of an accident, the damages have to be assessed separately as pecuniary damages and special damages. Pecuniary damages are those which the victim has actually incurred and which are capable of being calculated in terms of money; whereas non-pecuniary damages are those which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations. In order to Vishnu (Dar) vs Jitender (260/17 O.I. Area) on 4 January, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/114979208/ 6 MACT No 251/2018 Vishnu Vs. Jitender Page No. 10 of 29 appreciate two concepts pecuniary damages may include expenses incurred by the claimant: (i) medical attendance; (ii) loss of earning of profit up to the date of trial; (iii) other material loss. So far non- pecuniary damages are concerned, they may include (i) damages for mental and physical shock, pain and suffering, already suffered or likely to be suffered in future; (ii) damages to compensate for the loss of amenities of life which may include a variety of matters i.e. on account of injury the claimant may not be able to walk, run or sit; (iii) damages for the loss of expectation of life, i.e., on account of injury the normal longevity of the person concerned is shortened; (iv) inconvenience, hardship, discomfort, disappointment, frustration and mental stress in life." 17. Certain principles for delineating just compensation were enumerated in the case of Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Anr., (2011) 1 SCC 343, by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India. Following observations are relevant in the context: "40.General principles relating to compensation in injury cases 5. The provision of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act", for short) makes it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident. The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner. The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable. A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury. This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned. [See C.K. Subramania Iyer v. T. Kunhikuttan Nair [(1969) 3 SCC 64 : AIR 1970 SC 376] , R.D. MACT No 251/2018 Vishnu Vs. Jitender Page No. 11 o Hattangadi v. Pest Control (India) (P) Ltd. [(1995) 1 SCC 551 : 1995 SCC (Cri) 250] and Baker v. Willoughby [1970 AC 467 : (1970) 2 WLR 50 : (1969) 3 All ER 1528 (HL)] .] 6. The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following: Pecuniary damages (Special damages) (i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalisation, medicines, transportation, nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure. (ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising: (a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment; (b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability. (vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity). MACT No 251/2018 Vishnu Vs. Jitender Page No. 12 Assessment of non-pecuniary damages--Items (iv), (v) and (vi)--involves determination of lump sum amounts with reference to circumstances such as age, nature of injury/deprivation/disability suffered by the claimant and the effect thereof on the future life of the claimant. We may however note that in some cases, MACT No 251/2018 Vishnu Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd. 18. The above-said principles have been placed reliance upon in a recent judgment MACT No 251/2018 Vishnu Vs. Jitender Page No. 16 of 29 reported as Sidram Vs. The Divisional Manager United India Insurance Co. Ltd and Anr., arising out of SLP (Civil) no. 19277 of 2018 passed by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India (DOD : 16.11.2022). 19.
